newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE-"Club Med" countries see only good in EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-"Club Med" countries see only good in EMU.

text.p: If Europe's "Club Med" countries, Italy, Spain and Portugal, end up as bridesmaids at the wedding of monetary union, it will not be due to lack of ardour for the single currency.

While politicians in northern European Union member countries may debate the pros and cons of the loss of independence that a single currency implies, few dissenting voices are raised south of the Alps and Pyrenees.

In Rome, Madrid and Lisbon, leading political parties give loud support for their countries' ambitions to be among the elite which takes part in the launch of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in January 1999.

Portugal's small but vocal right-wing Popular Party is one of the few political groupings publicly to oppose EMU, but even some of its leading lights admit that the country probably has no option but to join if it can.
"There is really no other choice. If all the others join, then Portugal must go in too," said University of Lisbon professor Vasco D'Orey, one of the party's best known economists.

Even a wave of opposition protests in Italy, triggered by the centre-left government's budget plans, focuses on who bears the brunt of tax increases rather than questioning the need to slash the state deficit next year, as eligibility criteria for the single currency demand.
"There is still a view that EMU is a crock of gold and all the suffering is worth it," said one political analyst in Milan.
In Spain, the conviction that the country must win access to EMU is arguably the one political policy uniting Madrid's ruling centre-right Popular Party and its Socialist predecessors.
ODDS ON ADMISSION SHORTENING

Until a few months ago, the odds on Europe's southern flank making the cut for monetary union were very long, with budget deficits stubbornly large and inflation seemingly too high for the exacting economic tests set down for entry.

But signs that there will be some flexibility when EU members sit down in the spring of 1998 to decide who qualifies, together with genuine progress in putting economic houses in order, have suddenly put "Club Med" in with a chance.

Even Italy, which faces the toughest task of the three, has seen a sharp narrowing in the interest rate premium that it must pay to borrow money, as investor confidence grows in Rome's financial discipline.
CHEAP MONEY MAIN INCENTIVE
The economic reasons why southern flank countries are falling over themselves to join EMU can be summed up in two words -- cheaper money.
Joining Germany and France inside monetary union would put the Mediterranean countries on virtually an equal footing with Europe's economic powerhouses when it comes to raising cash.
Italy, Europe's most indebted country, stands to save huge sums as it sorts out the chaotic state finances which have been a millstone around the neck of an otherwise dynamic economy.
Economists calculate that the narrowing of Italy's interest rate differential to Germany has cut the government's bill on national debt by over $1 billion over the past year alone.

With a state debt equal to 120 percent of the annual output of the economy (GDP), each percentage point reduction in interest rates knocks the equivalent of 1.2 percent GDP off Rome's annual interest bill -- a colossal amount.

Political leaders may baulk at admitting it, but many local economists also say that the three countries -- comparatively recent converts to financial rectitude -- need the discipline of the single currency to go on applying the strict budgetary policies that are now bringing success.
"I doubt that without this pressure from monetary union that we would have the progress on the public finances that we have had," said former Portuguese finance minister Miguel Beleza.
"Limits on our ability to have the wrong policies are welcome," said Beleza, who has also served as governor of the central bank.

Being outside the inner core of monetary union could also hurt big, export-oriented companies within the three states, such as Italian car giant Fiat, by denying them cost savings as exchange rates disappear and borrowing charges fall.
POLITICAL PULL OVERPOWERING
But for southern Europe, EMU is far from being purely a question of economics.
Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres says Lisbon's main worry is that failure to qualify for monetary union would condemn the country to a European second division.

With the EU set to grow with the arrival of new members, countries such as Portugal, already geographically distant from the centre of affairs, risked being left with no voice and no way to influence decisions.
"There will be a centre in the new Europe and that centre will be based on the countries that belong to monetary union. We want to be part of that centre," he told Reuters.

For Spain, the European Union has been crucial to completing the country's evolution from an isolated, economic backwater under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, who died in 1975, to a self-confident and thrusting democracy.
Italy, too, has consistently punched above its international weight thanks to the EU, where it prides itself on being the master deal-maker.

"Without Italy, Europe would lack a major player, not just in terms of size but above all in ability to strike a balance between the various partners," wrote Fiat honorary chairman Giovanni Agnelli recently.
ECONOMIC RISK "SIGNFICANT"

But the near-unanimity amongst Spanish, Italian and Portuguese political leaders on the need to enter monetary union has served to mask the fact that membership could have a significant economic cost, some economists argue.

One London-based economist with an international investment house warned that Spain and Italy, in particular, could lose out by surrendering control over their exchange rates before their economies were fully prepared.

He argued that both countries suffered from severe rigidities in their labour markets as well as a burdensome bureaucracy that could condemn them to continuing high levels of unemployment within a system of fixed exchange rates.
"I am more concerned probably than others. There are risks to a too early participation without restructuring the supply side of the economy," said the economist who asked not to be named.
"There could be a significant (negative) impact on output and employment if Italy and Spain enter in the first group of countries," he warned.
